title: Making the Invisible Ownable
subtitle: Redesigning loan origination in the J.P. Morgan Global Private Bank

meta.label: Role
meta.value: Lead Product Designer — discovery to delivery

meta.label: Team
meta.value: Self-driven · 4 POs · Engineering · Credit Risk · Middle Office

value: The Global Private Bank spans USPB — 55 U.S. markets — and IPB across APAC, EMEA and LatAm: 1,000+ advisors, clients in 140+ countries, nine languages, 30+ regulators. Lending is one product line inside that footprint, used by client-facing and credit teams in every region.

I own two of its surfaces. The Loan Request App is the workflow where lenders apply for a loan on behalf of their clients. The Lending Workspace is the daily hub where lenders reach every other tool and workflow.

items.label: Where a deal starts
items.title: Loan Request App
items.desc: The intake workflow — client and facility, loan details, review — for SBL, Custom Credit and PLP tickets across USPB, EMEA, APAC and LatAm.

items.label: Where lenders live all day
items.title: Lending Workspace
items.desc: The hub tying together Deal Journey, Portfolio Health, Insights, Doc QC, Collateral Tools, Margin Call, Book Simulation, ILM and Approvals.

blocks.label: Loan Request App — the Client & facility step where a deal begins
Lending Workspace — the daily hub

blocks.value: My users sit along the whole chain: Bankers, SC Advisors, Lender Specialists, Credit Risk and Middle Office, senior and junior.

indexedSections.title: The brief, and why it was wrong

value: I was given a narrow mandate: the intake form is bad, clean up the Loan Request App to reduce rework. The trigger was a recurring complaint from Lender Specialists.

blocks.value: Half my loan requests bounce back. I redo them two or three times before Credit even looks.
The business read this as a UI problem. My first job was to test that assumption before designing anything.

blocks.label: The reframe
blocks.value: The form wasn't ugly. It was collecting the Banker's information but being measured against Credit's requirements — a handoff mismatch, not a UI mismatch.

indexedSections.title: Mapping a workflow nobody owned end to end

value: When I tried to map the current state I hit two gaps at once. No single person could describe the full origination chain — each role saw only their own segment and assumed the next one worked fine. And more fundamentally, my workspace had no shared source of truth to begin with: no documented information architecture, no defined personas. Everyone was designing and prioritising against their own mental model of who the user is and how the product is structured.
So before I could fix the workflow, I had to build the foundation nobody had built.

blocks.title: Build the missing source of truth

blocks.value: I interviewed lenders and domain owners across roles — embedding in advisor check-ins and morning meetings to reach client-facing users who are otherwise hard to pin down — and synthesised what I learned into two reference artefacts.

items.title: Lending Workspace IA
items.desc: A top-to-bottom, current-state map of the navigation hierarchy: L1 products, L2 apps, their sub-tabs and page-level controls. The first time anyone could see the whole system on one screen.

items.title: Lending personas
items.desc: Role-based personas across the journey — Banker, SC Advisor, Lender Specialist, Credit Risk, Middle Office, senior and junior variants — capturing goals, jobs to be done and pain points in the apps they actually use.

blocks.label: The Lending Workspace information architecture — the whole hierarchy on one screen
Lending personas — goals, activities and frustrations per role
Impact beyond my project
blocks.value: Both artefacts became a de-facto source of truth. The design team and product owners started referencing them in their own reviews and roadmaps — scaffolding for my discovery turned into shared infrastructure for the group.

With that shared map in place I could finally isolate where the rework happened. Instead of more one-on-one interviews, I put one person from each role in a room with a single anonymised loan request — a real-estate investor leveraging existing assets for a line of credit to acquire a new property — printed as a physical timeline on the wall.
Don't describe your job. Trace this specific deal, and put a red dot every time you had to stop and ask someone a question.

blocks.label: The deal timeline with every stop-and-ask marked — the dots clustered at the same three seams

blocks.value: The red dots clustered at the same three seams every time. The most consistent: requests arriving at Credit missing collateral and entity details the Banker was never asked for at intake — the asset basis and ownership structure Credit needs to size a securities- or property-backed facility.

blocks.label: What the seams cost — not-in-good-order submissions, mid-flow restarts, and manual handoffs
The baseline
blocks.value: To size the problem before designing, I ran a lightweight manual audit with Middle Office: 40 recent loan requests, ~60% bounced at least once, with the top two reasons matching two of the three seams. That number became my north star.

indexedSections.title: Manufacturing an owner for an unowned problem

value: The workflow spanned four teams across USPB and IPB, each region with its own regulators and its own roadmap. The products were disconnected because every product owner was so specialised: each owned a narrow slice deeply, with little visibility into the seams between slices. No one had authority over the whole chain, so "fix the intake" became a hot potato — the Loan Request App PO called it a Credit problem, Credit called it an intake problem.

blocks.title: Make the problem impossible to pass along

blocks.value: I turned the red-dot findings into a one-page Rework Map: three seams, the cost of each, and the two teams that touched it. Then I booked one 45-minute review with all four POs and the Credit Risk lead together — a meeting that had never happened, because they had only ever met pairwise.

blocks.label: The Rework Map — three seams, cost per seam, owning teams on a single page

blocks.value: Seeing the same three seams, quantified, in front of everyone at once made the potato impossible to pass. The Credit lead said the unlocking line:
If we just told them what we needed up front, we'd stop bouncing these.

blocks.label: What that bought me
blocks.value: A de-facto sponsor by evidence, not org chart.

blocks.title: Make alignment a habit, not a meeting

blocks.value: Because the teams were specialised and spread across regions — a live pilot was already running across USPB, EMEA and APAC — a single workshop wouldn't hold them together. So I built three lightweight recurring rituals.

items.title: Design office hours
items.desc: An open standing slot where any PO could bring a question, a request or a half-formed idea. One predictable door to knock on, and cross-team dependencies surfaced before they hardened into conflicts.

items.title: Socialised decisions
items.desc: I circulated the why behind each decision, not just the final screens, so no one was surprised in review. Shared rationale, not just shared artefacts.

items.title: Refinement calls
items.desc: I sat in on engineering refinement across initiatives, catching feasibility issues and cross-initiative overlaps in real time instead of after something had been built the wrong way.

blocks.label: Why it worked
blocks.value: In a specialised, multi-region org, alignment isn't a document — it's presence. Consistently reachable, consistently transparent, consistently present where the work got scoped, I became the connective tissue between owners each optimising their own slice.

blocks.title: Bring design upstream of the roadmap

value: The rituals kept day-to-day teams in sync, but they couldn't resolve the bigger fracture: the POs had no alignment on prioritisation across the portfolio. Every owner could defend their own slice, but no one could sequence the whole roadmap — initiation, fulfilment, monitoring, servicing, Workspace, data and shared services were all competing, un-normalised and un-sequenced.

Leadership convened a three-day in-person portfolio workshop at the Ohio HQ, and I travelled there as the only design representative in the room, alongside POs, journey owners, data, architecture and risk leads. Over three days we drove a single working artefact from initiative to epic to feature to persona to job-to-be-done to journey, routing, owner, dependency, size, sequence and change impact.

blocks.label: Three days at HQ as the only designer in the room

blocks.value: My role wasn't to take notes. It was to bring the design perspective into decisions that were otherwise about inventory, sizing and sequencing.

items.title: Showed concrete futures
items.desc: I presented three explorations of the Loan Request App side by side so leadership could evaluate directions concretely, not abstractly. The agenda literally read: use Yichun's prototypes as reference points.

items.title: Anchored in personas
items.desc: My IA and personas became the shared language for defining every feature's persona, journey and routing — keeping the conversation tied to user outcomes rather than system boundaries.

items.title: Shaped the Workspace model
items.desc: Persona-based views, work queues, and the list → action → launch → context → return pattern that would make the portfolio feel like one experience instead of ten apps.

blocks.value: The three explorations I put in front of them:

items.label: Exploration 1
items.title: One Request, Any Deal
items.desc: A single unified request with no SBL-versus-Custom fork — the split that caused mis-routed intake in the first place.

items.label: Exploration 2
items.title: AI Application Agent
items.desc: Fill the request by chatting: the system drafts the ticket from conversation rather than from a form.

items.label: Exploration 3
items.title: Collateral-First Builder
items.desc: Start from the client's assets; line size, rate and covenant headroom recalculate live as collateral changes.

blocks.label: The three future-vision proposals, side by side
Why it mattered
blocks.value: As the single design voice at the portfolio table, I moved design upstream of prioritisation — helping leadership choose which direction to invest in, rather than being handed a sequenced backlog to decorate. Design became an input to the roadmap, not an output of it.

Of the three proposals the boldest was the AI Application Agent — auto-populate and auto-size the whole request from a chat. The business loved it: fewer fields, faster. But prototype testing with two Lender Specialists exposed a trust wall.
If the system sizes it and it's wrong, it's still my name on the deal. I'll just redo it by hand to be safe.

blocks.label: The trap
blocks.value: Full automation would have recreated the exact rework it was meant to remove.

So I combined the strengths instead. One Request, Any Deal became the backbone, killing the fork that caused mis-routed intake. I borrowed the Collateral-First Builder's live recalculation to surface borrowing capacity early. And I treated the AI agent as an assist, not an autopilot — three moves designed for trust:

items.label: Transparency
items.title: Provenance on every value
items.desc: Every pre-filled or AI-suggested value carries a provenance chip: source system and as-of date.

items.label: Reversibility
items.title: The human keeps the pen
items.desc: One-click override with a required reason. Nothing the system proposes is beyond the user's reach.

items.label: Context flows forward
items.title: Explained, not suspicious
items.desc: Override reasons travel with the request to Credit, so an adjusted number arrives with its rationale attached.

blocks.label: A pre-filled field with its provenance chip, and the override-with-reason interaction
The rationale I'd defend in any review
blocks.value: In lending, accountability is personal and non-delegable. The cost-effective choice wasn't the most automated proposal — it was the one that made automation transparent and reversible, so it earned trust instead of demanding it.

indexedSections.title: Driving to ship without formal authority

blocks.value: No PO ran cover. I led discovery, aligned four teams, made the design calls and drove to build with no authority over any of them. What carried it was leading with artefacts rather than opinions.

items.title: Prototypes, not specs
items.desc: Clickable prototypes surfaced real feasibility. When Engineering flagged that one collateral field lived in a system they couldn't read in real time, I didn't fight it — I scoped v1 to the two seams we could fix and parked the third with written rationale.

items.title: Every trade-off anchored to the baseline
items.desc: Six in ten requests get redone, and we can prevent most of it upstream. That line from the 40-request audit carried the initiative through prioritisation whenever opinions competed.

blocks.label: Before and after — Credit's acceptance rules moved upstream into the Banker's intake moment
What testing told us to build, and what to fix in the copy

blocks.value: The regional variants shipped on one shared skeleton, with conditional logic injecting what each market required rather than forking the product.

blocks.label: One skeleton, four markets — USPB, EMEA, APAC and LatAm variants

value: Validate-at-source intake shipped into the Loan Request App with provenance chips and reason-coded overrides, and is now in multi-region pilot across USPB, EMEA and APAC.

NIGO — not in good order — is the firm's term for exactly the bounce-back rework I set out to reduce, which makes it the metric that most directly reflects the work. Measured against my discovery baseline of ~60% of requests bouncing at least once, ~22% is a substantial cut in first-pass rework. It's a programme-level result the redesign contributed to, alongside process and training changes.

blocks.label: What the usage mix confirms
blocks.value: A 19-week average of ~190 weekly active users, led by Lenders (43.8%), Analysts (16.9%) and Credit Middle Office (16.3%) — the exact roles, in the exact priority order, the personas were built around.

blocks.label: The pilot scorecard — NIGO, adoption, and the weekly-active role mix

blocks.value: The Lending Workspace became a more coherent daily hub along the way: the Deal Journey Tracker now integrates the eCQ credit-questionnaire workflow and has onboarded IPB SBL and Custom deals, giving end-to-end visibility across the seams I mapped in discovery. And the IA map and personas remain a source of truth the design team and product owners still reference.

blocks.label: The shipped Loan Request App

indexedSections.title: Ownership problems in a design costume

blocks.label: The takeaway
blocks.value: The hardest problems in a large organisation usually aren't design problems — they're ownership problems wearing a design costume. My contribution was making an unowned, invisible workflow visible and shared enough that the right decision became obvious to everyone at once.
Three moves proved repeatable beyond this project.

items.label: Move 1
items.title: When there's no shared source of truth, build it
items.desc: The IA and personas I created outlived the initiative and now anchor how the team designs and prioritises.

items.label: Move 2
items.title: When a problem has no owner, make it undeniable in a shared room
items.desc: Then keep it aligned through presence — office hours, socialised decisions, refinement calls — rather than hunting for authority that doesn't exist.

items.label: Move 3
items.title: When the portfolio can't agree on priority, bring design upstream
items.desc: Future-vision prototypes gave leadership something concrete to decide against, turning design into an input to the roadmap rather than an output of it.

blocks.label: What I'm still watching
blocks.value: Adoption is real but early, and I treat the numbers honestly. When Workspace showed a −10.8% week-over-week dip in active users I didn't wave it away — the open question is whether it's seasonality or an access-provisioning issue, and it's exactly the kind of signal I want instrumented rather than guessed.

What I'd do differently: wire real telemetry into the two targeted intake seams from day one, so NIGO improvement can be attributed cleanly to the design change, and so the parked third seam has quantified evidence ready when it comes up for prioritisation — rather than relying on a manual audit.
